decision.location: methods, lines 317-329; references, lines 1023-1027; Table 2, lines 1505-1507
decision.quote:
Sunk costs (Oppenheimer, Meyvis, & Davidenko, 2009). Sunk costs are those that have 

already been incurred and cannot be recovered (Knox & Inkster, 1968). Oppenheimer et al. 

(2009; adapted from Thaler, 1985) asked participants to imagine that they have tickets to see 

their favorite football team play an important game, but that it is freezing cold on the day of 

the game. Participants rated their likelihood of attending the game on a 9-point scale (1 = 

definitely stay at home, 9 = definitely go to the game). Participants were marginally more 

likely to go to the game if they had paid for the ticket than if the ticket had been free.
decision.reason: Klein et al. (2014) empirically re-test the sunk-cost scenario experiment from Oppenheimer, Meyvis, and Davidenko (2009, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 45, 867-872) as Effect 1 of their 13 replicated effects across 36 samples (N = 6,344 total; Table 2 reports original d = 0.23 and replication d = 0.27, t = 10.83, p < .001). Under the codebook replication-chain rule, Oppenheimer, Meyvis, and Davidenko (2009) is the proximate empirical study whose experimental operationalization (9-point likelihood scale for attending a freezing football game with a paid vs. free ticket, adapted from Thaler, 1985) and effect size are directly re-tested and compared in Table 2 (whereas the instructional manipulation check from the same paper was administered at the end of the session as a data quality measure and not analyzed here). This work is distinct from shipped row 1589 (Oppenheimer & Monin, 2009, Judgment and Decision Making, 10.1017/s1930297500001170, which is Effect 4 on the retrospective gambler's fallacy) and from all other 7 shipped rows (1554 Husnu & Crisp 2010; 1611 Nosek et al. 2002; 1715 Caruso et al. 2013; 1817 Schwarz et al. 1985; 1980 Tversky & Kahneman 1981; 2001 Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995; 2015 Carter et al. 2011) as well as sibling missing targets 5, 6, and 7. Prior adjudication also confirmed blind_right; corrected_value is formatted with record_type:'replication', outcome:'cannot_be_determined', and doi:'' because no DOI is printed in the source text.

decision.location: methods, lines 421-437; references, lines 972-976; Table 2, lines 1501-1503
decision.quote:
Norm of reciprocity (Hyman & Sheatsley, 1950). When confronted with a decision about 

allowing or denying the same behavior to an ingroup and outgroup, people may feel an 

obligation to reciprocity, or consistency in their evaluation of the behaviors (Hyman & 

Sheatsley, 1950). In the original study, American participants answered two questions: 

whether communist countries should allow American reporters in and allow them to report 

the news back to American papers and whether America should allow communist reporters 

into the United States and allow them to report back to their papers. Participants reported 

more support for allowing communist reporters into America when that question was asked 

after the question about allowing American reporters into the communist countries.
decision.reason: Klein et al. (2014) empirically re-test the norm of reciprocity question-order effect from Hyman and Sheatsley (1950) as Effect 6 of their 13 replicated effects across 36 samples, reporting original and replication effect sizes and statistical tests in Table 2 (original d = 0.16, replication d = 0.29, chi-square = 135.3, p < .001). None of the 8 shipped rows (1554, 1589, 1611, 1715, 1817, 1980, 2001, 2015) nor sibling missing targets (0, 6, 7) represent Hyman and Sheatsley (1950). Prior adjudication confirmed blind_right; corrected_value uses record_type:'replication', outcome:'cannot_be_determined', and doi:'' since no DOI is printed in the source text.

decision.location: methods, lines 450-466; references, line 1039; Table 2, line 1458
decision.quote:
Allowed/Forbidden (Rugg, 1941). Question phrasing can influence responses. Rugg (1941) 

found that respondents were less likely to endorse forbidding speeches against democracy 

than they were to not endorse allowing speeches against democracy. Respondents in the 

United States were asked, in one condition, if the U.S. should allow speeches against 

democracy or, in another condition, whether the U.S. should forbid speeches against 

democracy. 62 percent of participants indicated “No” when asked if speeches against 

democracy should be allowed, but only 46 percent indicated “Yes” when asked if these 

speeches should be forbidden. In the replication, the words “The United States” were 

replaced with the name of the country the study was administered in.
decision.reason: Klein et al. (2014) empirically re-test the allowed/forbidden question wording asymmetry from Rugg (1941, Public Opinion Quarterly, 5, 91-92) as Effect 7 of their 13 replicated effects across 36 samples, reporting original and replication effect sizes and statistical tests in Table 2 (original d = 0.65, replication d = 1.90, chi-square = 3088.7, p < .001). Rugg (1941) is completely distinct from shipped row 1817 (Schwarz et al., 1985, Public Opinion Quarterly, 10.1086/268936, which is Effect 5 on low- vs. high-category frequency scales for TV viewing) and from all other shipped rows (1554, 1589, 1611, 1715, 1980, 2001, 2015) and sibling missing targets (0, 5, 7). Prior adjudication confirmed blind_right; corrected_value uses record_type:'replication', outcome:'cannot_be_determined', and doi:'' since no DOI is printed in the source text.

decision.location: methods, lines 468-484; references, lines 994-996; Table 2, line 1497
decision.quote:
Quote Attribution (Lorge & Curtis, 1936). The source of information has a great impact on 

how that information is perceived and evaluated. Lorge and Curtis (1936) examined how an 

identical quote would be perceived if it was attributed to a liked or disliked individual. 

Participants were asked to rate their agreement with a list of quotations. The quotation of 

interest was, “I hold it that a little rebellion, now and then, is a good thing, and as necessary 

in the political world as storms are in the physical world.” In one condition the quote was 

attributed to Thomas Jefferson, a liked individual, and in the other it was attributed to 

Vladimir Lenin, a disliked individual. More agreement was observed when the quote was 

attributed to Jefferson than Lenin (reported in Moskowitz, 2004).
decision.reason: Klein et al. (2014) empirically re-test the quote attribution effect from Lorge and Curtis (1936, Journal of Social Psychology, 7, 386-402) as Effect 8 of their 13 replicated effects across 36 samples, reporting the replication results in Table 2 (replication d = 0.33, t = 12.79, p < .001). Under the codebook primary-study rule, Lorge and Curtis (1936) is the primary original empirical study rather than the secondary textbook (Moskowitz, 2004) in which it was summarized. None of the 8 shipped rows (1554, 1589, 1611, 1715, 1817, 1980, 2001, 2015) nor sibling missing targets (0, 5, 6) represent Lorge and Curtis (1936). Prior adjudication confirmed blind_right; corrected_value uses record_type:'replication', outcome:'cannot_be_determined', and doi:'' since no DOI is printed in the source text.

decision.quote: The purpose is to replicate and extend Ambulkar et al.’s (2015) work testing resource reconfiguration as a mediator of the supply chain disruption/firm resilience relationship and testing risk management infrastructure as a moderator. This study extends the work of Ambulkar in that it uses analysis of survey data gathered from manufacturing firms during an actual disruption event (COVID-19).
decision.reason: The candidate target extracted from the abstract ('Ambulkar et al.', 2015) is the exact same original study already represented by shipped row input_row_index 840 (doi_o: 10.1016/j.jom.2014.11.002, authors_o: 'Ambulkar; Blackhurst; Grawe', year_o: '2014', title_o: 'Firm's resilience to supply chain disruptions: Scale development and empirical examination'). Crossref bibliography metadata for 10.1016/j.jom.2014.11.002 confirms that Saurabh Ambulkar, Jennifer Blackhurst, and Scott Grawe's article in the Journal of Operations Management (Vol. 33-34, Issue 1, pp. 111-122) was published online on November 18, 2014 ahead of the January 2015 volume issue, which explains the 2014 vs. 2015 publication year discrepancy between the DOI metadata in shipped row 840 and the in-text citation ('Ambulkar et al.’s (2015) work') in the replicating paper's abstract. Furthermore, the replicating paper's title ('A COVID replication and extension of firms’ resilience to supply chain disruptions') directly mirrors the title of 10.1016/j.jom.2014.11.002. No prior adjudication/state files existed for this work. Because the single replicated target is already represented by shipped row 840, the candidate missing_row is redundant and shipped_right applies.

corrected_value.title: Self-Censorship of Regime Support in Authoritarian States: Evidence from List Experiments in China.

decision.quote: We examined sensitive questions on political trust and regime support in China using indirect methods. We replicated previous list experiment results confirming that a majority trusts the central government despite overreports. We also conducted novel list experiments on trust in local government and support for removal of the presidential term limit and found evidence of overreporting for both.
decision.reason: In the abstract (line 23), Nicholson and Huang explicitly state that they 'replicated previous list experiment results confirming that a majority trusts the central government despite overreports' on political trust and regime support in China. In the paper's full reference list (lines 40-78), the sole empirical study conducting list experiments on regime support/political trust in China is Robinson and Tannenberg (2019), 'Self-Censorship of Regime Support in Authoritarian States: Evidence from List Experiments in China,' Research & Politics 6(3): 1-9 (line 68; the only other list-experiment citations, Blair et al. 2020 and Blair & Imai 2012, are general methodological papers). This target is completely distinct from shipped row input_row_index 150 (Tang, Wenfang, 2016, 'Populist Authoritarianism: Chinese Political Culture and Regime Sustainability,' Oxford University Press monograph, doi_o: 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780190205782.001.0001, reference list line 74). No prior adjudication/state files existed for this work, and no DOI is printed for Robinson and Tannenberg (2019) in the supplied source text, so blind_right applies with doi:''.
